fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A crowdsourced map of a strange country", "body": "Mark Steeves came on to talk about Esoteric America, the new show he launched with Chad Stemke after recording five episodes before releasing any of them. The premise is that listeners, not experts, should be the guests. Mark tells Chance Garton he can only speak for Connecticut, so he wants local researchers everywhere filling in the map with mounds, native history, Tartaria, colonial history and oddities like the one footed snorkel monster. He points to Andrea breaking down Baudette, Minnesota and Jack Asgard breaking down the Inland Empire as the model for what the show is trying to build."}, {"title": "What S.E.E.E.N. actually asks you to do", "body": "The pamphlet Mark wrote stands for the Synchromistic Exploration of the Ever Expanding Now, and he frames it as a travel guide to wherever you already are. It grew out of his frustration with the Randonautica app, which never worked in an area with no phone service. The kit is a pair of dice, a compass, a map, a notebook and pen, a camera, a backpack and a cup. The cup holds the dice so you can shake them while driving, with odds meaning left and evens meaning right, provoking randomness until you are genuinely lost."}, {"title": "Dreamwalking instead of sleepwalking", "body": "Mark argues that most of us are sleepwalkers and that dreamwalking is the deliberate opposite, a way of waking up to a reality that is always there the way dreams are. He believes the land itself carries an energetic imprint from the people who lived here for thousands of years, and that those layers sit under only four hundred years of newer history like soil turned over by a farmer. You can connect with ancestors who share no genealogy with you, he says, through the dirt, the plants, the animals and the common ground you both stand on."}, {"title": "Why the psychedelic push looks suspicious", "body": "Chance raises the question of why psychedelics are suddenly being moved into pharmaceutical and psychiatric territory, and suggests a hyper materialistic culture is grabbing them as another experience to collect. Mark answers that science is trying to quantify spirituality by breaking plants down into molecules, and speculates the real goal is finding a chemical bridge into augmented digital reality, noting synthetic compounds are easier to program. His stronger claim is that people have it backwards. The experience is in you and the mushroom only activates it. He compares his book to a swing set next to the roller coaster of ayahuasca."}, {"title": "Breaking routine, gratitude and omens", "body": "The practical heart of the conversation is that our problems live inside our routines, so stepping out of the daily pie chart of hours creates room to see them. Mark asks people to set aside real time, express gratitude, and log every object, omen and occurrence, because a pattern surfaces after a few outings. He teaches a walking meditation of matching steps to breath, and describes the drifting state you enter while driving as a doorway to synchronicity. Chance closes with the copy of The Alchemist by Paulo Coelho that reached him in Chicago days after he asked for it."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Mark Steeves, host and co-host of many epic podcasts, including his flagship show My Family Thinks I'm Crazy, returns to InnerVerse to talk about his new projects, Esoteric America and S.E.E.E.N. Mark is quickly becoming a leader in the world of synchromystic explorations, connecting to Gaia consciousness, and of course, the conspiracy & spirituality that we love to research.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Reading signs on an ordinary morning walk", "body": "Chance Garton describes trying Mark's SEEEN method on a walk to a creek where he practices Qigong. He finds a pen at the trailhead pointing toward his destination, a baby snapping turtle in the path, and a drawing pencil resting on a plaque inscribed with Deuteronomy 8:7. Chance reads the turtle as a nudge to come out of the shell of routine, which he calls a protection against randomness, and the pencil as an invitation to make time for drawing. Mark adds that discarded objects carry a story, since someone's thoughts and intentions once went into them."}, {"title": "What lies below the surface of a place", "body": "Mark Steeves notes that learning about the place you live may turn up things you never wanted to know. Chance Garton then recounts two unsettling encounters with strangers at his favorite creek, a year apart, and concludes the spot is no longer his. Mark treats the episode as exactly the kind of experience the SEEEN method is meant to surface, arguing there is a purpose behind what happens and that it is worth examining. He suggests families reclaiming such spots could change how they are used, while Chance reflects that hidden struggles sit beneath polished appearances almost everywhere."}, {"title": "Sexual energy, masculinity and modern culture", "body": "In a frank stretch both men share personal and openly contested views on sexuality and gender roles. Mark Steeves says his interest in pornography faded once he entered a committed relationship and argues the industry exploits damaged people. Chance Garton suggests sexuality has long been wielded against society and that men are conditioned to find the most taboo things the most arousing. Drawing on the traditional Chinese medicine idea of jing, Chance argues that losing this essence weakens masculinity. Both also voice critical opinions on homosexuality and feminism, which they acknowledge many listeners will find controversial or disagree with."}, {"title": "Animals as messengers on the journey", "body": "Mark Steeves reads from Dancing with the Wheel, the medicine wheel workbook, explaining that the turtle invites care for oneself and the whole community. He recommends books such as Animal Spirit and Medicine Cards for interpreting encounters. Mark then tells of finding a great blue heron with a broken leg alongside his girlfriend and getting it to rehabilitation on a Sunday evening, an experience that now graces the cover of his book. Chance Garton links the heron to Qigong forms modeled on animals, and Mark recalls a childhood love of animal styles in martial arts."}, {"title": "Mapping a hidden America from the ground up", "body": "Mark Steeves explains how explorers can turn notes from each outing into a personal map, using a Google Maps screenshot and a tool like Canva to pin animals, buildings, plants or minerals. He envisions Esoteric America eventually offering a clickable map of every place the show covers, and argues people should make their own maps rather than relying on official ones. Chance Garton observes that old maps blended geography with myth and legend. Mark describes Nashville's bicentennial mall as an acoustic structure and explains why the show's cover art features a turtle, nodding to the name Turtle Island."}]

It's another thing to be in the right state of mind and awareness to totally witness the beauty that is that creature and it's sharing its presence with you.", "author": "Mark Steeves", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/89d9dfb0-79ac-4c32-9bde-a0b40a334110/MARK-STEEVES.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Instead of just having all of these segmented, unconnected stories, you create a cohesive storyboard almost through the map.", "author": "Mark Steeves", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/89d9dfb0-79ac-4c32-9bde-a0b40a334110/MARK-STEEVES.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "A map doesn't have to be something that you just use to find places. It could be something that you create to help you reimagine the reality that you're in.", "author": "Mark Steeves", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/89d9dfb0-79ac-4c32-9bde-a0b40a334110/MARK-STEEVES.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We have these really rich maps from our ancient past that show people not just what actually physically is there, but what the experiences of a place are.", "author": "Mark Steeves", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/89d9dfb0-79ac-4c32-9bde-a0b40a334110/MARK-STEEVES.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The life I lived previous to podcasting, I would go from job to job to job, and skills I got at one job would blend into the skills I used in the next job.
